meta.forecast_pub: The Budget and Economic Outlook: 2020 to 2030 (Jan 2020), pub. 51135
meta.source: Bureau of Economic Analysis, BLS, Federal Reserve via FRED; Congressional Budget Office; author's calculations.
meta.discussion:
Set CBO's January-2020 baseline beside what actually happened and the surprises sort into one clean pattern: the real economy turned out close to — even a little better than — what was expected, while the nominal economy is almost unrecognizable. On this evidence the pandemic delivered a lasting nominal shock far more than a lasting real one.

Start with the real side. After the deepest and fastest recession in modern memory, real GDP did not merely claw back to its pre-COVID path but pushed slightly above it, and the job market returned faster and tighter than almost anyone projected — unemployment round-tripped to roughly the low rate CBO had penciled in, rather than grinding back over years as it did after 2008. That is the dog that didn't bark: the permanent "scarring" of output and employment that the 2008–2015 experience taught us to fear simply does not show up in the aggregates. Shown only the real-GDP and unemployment lines, a 2020 forecaster would feel broadly vindicated — having lived through a wild detour to get there.

Show that same forecaster the price level and the path of interest rates, and the world is unrecognizable. The single largest break with the forecast is prices: the 2021–2023 surge stepped the price level well above anything in the baseline and never reversed — disinflation brought down the rate of increase, not the level of prices. The bulk of the gap between forecast and actual nominal GDP is this price overshoot rather than extra real output. The second great miss is interest rates. CBO's baseline encoded the low-for-long regime everyone assumed in early 2020; instead the most aggressive tightening cycle in four decades pushed short rates and the ten-year yield far above the projected path. The zero-rate era that framed a decade of macro thinking ended abruptly.

These are not independent surprises — they are two faces of one story. Enormous fiscal and monetary support met a supply-constrained reopening; demand snapped back hard (the strong real recovery and the tight labor market), that strength collided with disrupted supply (the inflation overshoot), and the overshoot forced the hiking cycle (the rates miss). The robust real economy and the nominal explosion are the same demand-driven event seen from different angles, not a run of unrelated luck.

Beneath the aggregates the composition shifted too — the mix of consumption, investment, and trade did not settle back into its old grooves — but the headline reading is simple and worth holding onto: measured against the last forecast made before the world changed, we arrived at roughly the real economy that was expected, resting on a permanently higher price level and a permanently higher structure of interest rates.
